newsitem.title: NICARAGUA: Nicaragua's Aleman calls for meeting with Ortega.
newsitem.headline: Nicaragua's Aleman calls for meeting with Ortega.

text.p: Nicaraguan President-elect Arnoldo Aleman on Friday said he would ask to meet with Sandinista opponent Daniel Ortega once Ortega recognizes Aleman's victory in last month's elections.

Aleman, the right-wing former mayor of Managua, told reporters the meeting would be to reach an agreement on the country's future governability, which analysts have said was threatened by the hostility between the two bitter rivals.
Ortega, a former president and leader of the left-wing Sandinista Front, refused to recognize Aleman's victory, saying the voting was tainted with fraud.

The Supreme Election Council (CSE), Nicaragua's highest election authority, was expected to soon announce the official winners of the elections, which would end more than a month of post-vote squabbling.

"Immediately after Daniel recognizes our triumph I'm willing to meet with him," Aleman said. "There has to be an agreement, a consensus, between the country's two principal powers, as are the Liberal Alliance and the Sandinista Front."
The CSE also will rule on a Sandinista appeal for new elections in two populous provinces because of alleged electoral fraud and irregularities.

CSE official Ana Maria Gutierrez on Wednesday told reporters the council's final verdict on Friday will not significantly change the provisional results, which gave Aleman an easy 51 percent to 37.7 percent win over Ortega.

Ortega said he will recognize the "legality" but not the "legitimacy" of a future Aleman government, and he said there could be a deepening political crisis if the CSE upheld the results as preliminarily reported.

Ortega's rebellion against the results led to fears over the future governability of Nicaragua because the second-place Sandinistas still wield considerable power, backed by a boisterous base of supporters willing to march in the streets.
The Sandinistas won 40 percent of the seats in the National Assembly and 51 city councils and they remained a major force within labor unions, police and the army.
